analysis.one_liner: Reinstates expired taxes on oil, chemical, and large corporations to fund toxic waste cleanups.
analysis.headline: The bill to make polluting industries pay again for toxic waste cleanups never got a committee vote and died when the 114th Congress ended in January 2017.
analysis.plain_summary: Since 1995, companies have not paid the special taxes that used to fill the Superfund trust fund, the federal fund that pays to clean up the nation's worst toxic waste sites. Instead, cleanups have been paid for out of general taxpayer money. This bill would bring back those taxes: an excise tax on crude oil and petroleum products and on hazardous chemicals, plus a small corporate income tax of 0.12% on very large corporate income, both through the end of 2020. It was sent to the House Ways and Means Committee, which never acted on it, and it expired when the Congress ended.
analysis.who_benefits: Ordinary taxpayers, who currently foot the bill for Superfund cleanups through general revenues, and communities living near toxic waste sites, who depend on the fund being solvent. Local governments that share cleanup costs also benefit.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Taxpayers and communities near toxic sites

how_it_helps.text: Reinstates the Hazardous Substance Superfund financing rate, the excise tax on crude oil, petroleum products, and hazardous chemicals that expired at the end of 1995, applying it from enactment through December 31, 2020.

Restores a corporate environmental income tax of 0.12% on the portion of a corporation's alternative minimum taxable income above $2 million, exempting regulated investment companies and real estate investment trusts, through taxable years beginning before January 1, 2021.

The money raised goes to the Hazardous Substance Superfund trust fund (section 9507 of the tax code), shifting cleanup funding from general taxpayers back to the companies whose products created the waste sites.

analysis.who_pays: Oil refiners, chemical manufacturers, and large corporations, which would again pay the excise and corporate environmental taxes they have not paid since 1995. Some of the excise tax could be passed through to consumers in fuel and chemical prices.

drawbacks.text: Excise taxes on crude oil and petroleum products are largely passed through to prices, so consumers would pay somewhat more at the pump and for petroleum-based goods while the tax is in effect.
The taxes would be temporary, ending after December 31, 2020, so the underlying question of permanent funding for Superfund cleanups would return.

The corporate environmental income tax applies to all corporations with more than $2 million in alternative minimum taxable income, not only the companies responsible for waste sites, so some firms with no connection to toxic waste would pay it.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit is a direct one: money for cleaning up toxic waste sites comes from the industries whose products created the pollution instead of from every taxpayer. The cost is a modest tax increase on oil, chemical, and large corporate income, part of which may show up in consumer prices. Weighing those, the bill puts the funding burden back on the parties that Superfund was originally designed to charge, and the temporary, expiring nature of the taxes is a fair criticism of its design.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was referred to the House Ways and Means Committee the day it was introduced, the committee never took it up, and it died when the 114th Congress ended in January 2017.

narrative.text: Rep. Frank Pallone introduced the bill on June 15, 2015, joined by Reps. Blumenauer and Pascrell, all Democrats.
The same day, the bill was referred to the House Committee on Ways and Means, the committee with jurisdiction over tax bills.
No further action was ever taken: the action history shows no hearing, no markup, no committee vote, and no floor vote for the remainder of the Congress.
The bill expired when the 114th Congress ended on January 3, 2017, meaning it would have to be reintroduced from scratch in the next Congress.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Oil, chemical, and other large corporations came out ahead: they continued to pay none of the Superfund taxes, and the cost of cleaning up toxic waste sites stayed on general taxpayers rather than shifting back to industry.

for.name: Rep. Frank Pallone Jr.
for.what_they_did: Introduced the Superfund Polluter Pays Act and referred it to Ways and Means.

against.name: House Ways and Means Committee Republican leadership
against.role: Committee with jurisdiction over the bill
against.what_they_did: Took no action on the bill after referral: no hearing, no markup, no vote in the two years remaining in the Congress.

against.name: Kevin Brady
against.role: Chair, House Ways and Means Committee
against.what_they_did: As chair of the committee holding the bill, never scheduled it for committee consideration, leaving it to die at the end of the Congress.

sides.party_line_note: The sponsor and all three cosponsors were House Democrats, and the Republican-controlled Ways and Means Committee never moved the bill, so support and inaction split along party lines.

industries.note: The bill reinstates the excise tax on crude oil and petroleum products that refiners and importers have not paid since 1995, money that would go to toxic waste cleanup. Refiners historically opposed its return because the tax raises their input costs, part of which reaches consumers.

The Hazardous Substance Superfund financing rate applies to hazardous chemicals as well as petroleum, so chemical makers would again pay into the cleanup fund their products helped fill. The industry's interest in avoiding the tax runs against taxpayers who otherwise pay for cleanups.
The 0.12% corporate environmental income tax on alternative minimum taxable income above $2 million falls on large corporations generally, restoring a tax they have not owed since the mid-1990s.

industries.industry: Environmental cleanup contractors and state co-funders of Superfund sites
industries.note: A replenished Superfund trust fund means more funded cleanups, which supports remediation work and relieves states and localities that share cleanup costs. Their interest runs alongside residents near waste sites.
